tips.title: Minutes are not seconds
tips.body: $Q = It$ needs time in **seconds**. Five minutes is 300 s, four minutes 240 s. Convert on the line before you substitute, and a whole class of lost marks disappears.

tips.title: Ammeter in, voltmeter across
tips.body: An **ammeter** goes **in series**, so the current it measures flows through it. A **voltmeter** goes **across** the component. Questions ask this constantly, and *in parallel with the component* is the same answer.

tips.title: Thermistor and lamp go opposite ways
tips.body: Hotter **filament lamp** → resistance **up**. Hotter **thermistor** → resistance **down**. They are easy to confuse and questions rely on it, so learn them as a contrasting pair rather than separately.

tips.title: Never read resistance off a gradient
tips.body: On an I–V graph the gradient is $\frac{1}{R}$, so steeper means **less** resistance. Instead of remembering which way round, read $V$ and $I$ at one point and calculate $R = V/I$. It works on curves too.

tips.title: Through the origin is part of the answer
tips.body: *A straight line* is not proportionality; **a straight line through the origin** is. When describing the graph for an ohmic resistor, those three extra words are usually the difference between one mark and two.

steps.title: Charge, current and the equation that links them
steps.body:
For electrical charge to flow through a **closed circuit**, the circuit must include a **source of potential difference** — a cell or a power supply. Without one, nothing flows.

**Electric current is a flow of electrical charge.** More precisely, the size of the current is the **rate of flow of charge**: how much charge passes a point each second.

$$\text{charge flow} = \text{current} \times \text{time} \qquad Q = It$$

- charge flow, $Q$, in **coulombs, C**
- current, $I$, in **amperes, A** (*amp* is accepted)
- time, $t$, in **seconds, s**

The time must be in **seconds**. A question in minutes is a question that wants you to multiply by 60 first, and forgetting is the single commonest arithmetic loss here.

One more fact, and it is the foundation of everything in the next topic:

$$\textbf{A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop.}$$

Charge is not used up as it goes round. A lamp does not consume current — it transfers energy. The same current that leaves the cell returns to it.

steps.title: Circuit symbols
steps.body:
Circuit diagrams use **standard symbols**, and you must be able to **draw and interpret** them. Marks are lost for symbols that are nearly right, so learn the details:

- A **cell** is one **long thin** line and one **short thick** line. The long line is the positive terminal. Two or more cells together make a **battery**.
- A **lamp** is a circle with a **cross** in it, drawn corner to corner.
- A **resistor** is a plain **rectangle** — not a zigzag, which is the American symbol.
- A **switch** is a line that lifts away from one of two dots.
- An **ammeter** is a circle with **A**, a **voltmeter** a circle with **V**.
- A **diode** is a **triangle pointing at a bar**. The triangle points the way the current can flow.
- A **thermistor** is a resistor with a **diagonal line** through it; an **LDR** is a resistor in a circle with **two arrows pointing in**.

The two meters are connected differently, and this is asked constantly:

- An **ammeter** goes **in series** — in the loop, so the current it measures passes through it.
- A **voltmeter** goes **in parallel**, **across** the component whose potential difference you want.

steps.title: Potential difference, current and resistance
steps.body:
The current through a component depends on **both** the **resistance** of the component and the **potential difference** across it.

$$\textbf{The greater the resistance, the smaller the current for a given potential difference.}$$

$$V = IR$$

- potential difference, $V$, in **volts, V**
- current, $I$, in **amperes, A**
- resistance, $R$, in **ohms, Ω**

Questions are set using the term **potential difference**, but you get credit for either *potential difference* or *voltage*.

steps.title: Components whose resistance changes
steps.body:
For **some** resistors the value of $R$ stays **constant**; for others it **changes as the current changes**. Knowing which is which is the point of this section.

**Ohmic conductor** (a resistor at constant temperature). The current is **directly proportional** to the potential difference, so the resistance stays **constant** as the current changes. Its graph of current against potential difference is a **straight line through the origin**.

**Filament lamp.** Its resistance **increases as the temperature of the filament increases**. A bigger current heats the filament more, so the resistance rises and the graph **curves over**, getting less steep.

**Diode.** The current flows in **one direction only**. In the reverse direction the diode has a **very high resistance**, so almost no current flows.

**Thermistor.** Its resistance **decreases as the temperature increases** — the opposite way round to the filament lamp, which is why they are easy to confuse. Used in a **thermostat**: as the room warms, the thermistor's resistance falls, the current rises, and the circuit switches the heating off.

**LDR** (light-dependent resistor). Its resistance **decreases as light intensity increases**. Used to **switch lights on when it gets dark**: less light means more resistance, and the circuit responds.

The two sensors are worth learning as a pair, because they work the same way: *more of the thing, less resistance*.

steps.title: The two required practicals
steps.body:
Two required practicals belong to this section, and both are examinable in detail.

**Required practical 3 — factors affecting resistance.** Use circuit diagrams to set up circuits and investigate:

- the **length of a wire** at constant temperature;
- **combinations of resistors in series and parallel**.

Method for the wire: connect the wire into a circuit with an **ammeter in series** and a **voltmeter across the wire**. Measure the current and potential difference for several lengths, and calculate $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ at each. The resistance is **directly proportional to length**, so the graph of resistance against length is a **straight line through the origin**.

The phrase **at constant temperature** is there for a reason: a current warms the wire, and a warmer wire has a higher resistance, which would spoil the result. So use a **low current**, and switch off between readings.

**Required practical 4 — I–V characteristics.** Use circuit diagrams to construct circuits and investigate the **I–V characteristics** of a **filament lamp**, a **diode** and a **resistor at constant temperature**.

The circuit is the same each time: the component, an **ammeter in series** with it, a **voltmeter across** it, and a way of varying the potential difference. Record current against potential difference and plot the graph. To get the negative half, **reverse the connections** to the supply.

steps.title: Going deeper: reading an I-V graph
steps.body:
**The graph is drawn current against potential difference**, so the **gradient is not the resistance** — it is $\frac{1}{R}$. A **steeper** line means a **smaller** resistance. This catches a lot of people, and the safe method is never to use the gradient at all: pick a point on the graph, read off $V$ and $I$, and calculate $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$.

**Explaining the three shapes.**

- **Resistor at constant temperature** — a straight line through the origin. Current is **directly proportional** to potential difference, so $R$ is **constant**. *Through the origin* is part of the answer: a straight line that misses the origin is not proportionality.
- **Filament lamp** — the line curves over, getting **less steep** as the potential difference rises. A larger current makes the filament **hotter**, and a hotter filament has a **higher resistance**, so the current rises less than proportionally. Because it is symmetrical, the graph is an S shape through the origin.
- **Diode** — almost **no current** in the reverse direction, because the resistance that way is **very high**, then a sharp rise in the forward direction. The graph is not symmetrical, and that asymmetry is the whole point.

**Why a hotter filament resists more.** The atoms in the metal vibrate more when it is hotter, so the electrons collide with them more often and find it harder to get through. You are not required to give that mechanism, but it makes the fact memorable rather than arbitrary.

**Thermistor or filament lamp?** They change the opposite ways, and questions exploit it:

- **Filament lamp**: hotter → resistance **up**.
- **Thermistor**: hotter → resistance **down**.

**Getting the units right.** $Q = It$ needs time in **seconds**; a question in minutes or hours is testing that conversion. And write **potential difference** in preference to *voltage* — both score, but the mark schemes are written in the first.

**Same current everywhere.** In a single loop the current is the same at every point. So if a question gives you a reading from one ammeter in a series circuit, you already know every other ammeter in that loop.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Charge flows only in a **closed circuit** containing a **source of potential difference**.
- Current is the **rate of flow of charge**: $Q = It$, with $Q$ in **coulombs**, $I$ in **amperes**, $t$ in **seconds**.
- **Convert minutes to seconds** before using $Q = It$.
- **A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop.**
- $V = IR$: potential difference in **volts**, resistance in **ohms**.
- **The greater the resistance, the smaller the current** for a given potential difference.
- An **ammeter** goes **in series**; a **voltmeter** goes **across** the component.
- A **resistor at constant temperature** is ohmic: current is **proportional** to pd, so $R$ is constant and the graph is a **straight line through the origin**.
- A **filament lamp's** resistance **increases** as it gets hotter, so its graph **curves over**.
- A **diode** conducts in **one direction only**, with a **very high resistance** in reverse.
- A **thermistor's** resistance **falls as temperature rises** — used in thermostats.
- An **LDR's** resistance **falls as light intensity rises** — used to switch lights on at dusk.
- On an I–V graph the gradient is $\frac{1}{R}$, so **steeper means less resistance**. Read off a point and divide instead.

questions.prompt: A 12 V supply is connected to a resistor. The current is 0.5 A. Find the resistance, then find the charge that flows in 4 minutes, and state what the current would be if the resistance were doubled.
questions.solution: The resistance is found using the equation potential difference equals current times resistance. Rearranging gives resistance equals potential difference divided by current, so the resistance is twelve divided by nought point five, which is twenty four ohms. To find the charge, the time must first be converted into seconds. Four minutes is four times sixty, which is two hundred and forty seconds. Using charge flow equals current times time, the charge is nought point five times two hundred and forty, which is one hundred and twenty coulombs. If the resistance were doubled to forty eight ohms with the same twelve volt supply, the current would be twelve divided by forty eight, which is nought point two five amperes. This is half the original current, which is expected because for a fixed potential difference the current is inversely proportional to the resistance, so doubling the resistance halves the current.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The resistance.**

$$R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{12}{0.5} = 24\ \Omega$$

**The charge.** Convert the time **first**:

$$4 \text{ minutes} = 4 \times 60 = 240 \text{ s}$$

$$Q = It = 0.5 \times 240 = 120 \text{ C}$$

**Doubling the resistance.** With the same 12 V supply and $R = 48\ \Omega$:

$$I = \frac{12}{48} = 0.25 \text{ A}$$

That is **half** the original current — as expected, because for a fixed potential difference the current is **inversely proportional** to resistance. Saying *why* the answer halves is worth the last mark on its own; a bare 0.25 A does not show you knew it had to.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the I-V characteristic of a filament lamp. Name the instruments and say where each is connected, describe the readings you would take, and explain the shape of the graph you would obtain.
questions.solution: The lamp is connected in a circuit with a cell or power supply and a way of varying the potential difference across it. An ammeter is connected in series with the lamp so that the current through the lamp passes through the ammeter, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel across the lamp so that it measures the potential difference across it. The potential difference is increased in steps, and at each step the readings on the ammeter and the voltmeter are recorded. To obtain the negative half of the graph, the connections to the supply are reversed and the readings are repeated. A graph of current against potential difference is then plotted. The graph is a curve that passes through the origin and becomes less steep as the potential difference increases, making an S shape overall. The reason is that a larger current makes the filament hotter, and the resistance of a filament lamp increases as its temperature increases, so each additional volt produces less additional current than the one before.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The circuit.**

- The **lamp**, with a supply and a way of **varying the potential difference**.
- An **ammeter in series** with the lamp, so the current through the lamp passes through it.
- A **voltmeter in parallel**, **across** the lamp.

**The readings.** Increase the potential difference in steps and record the **ammeter and voltmeter** readings at each. Then **reverse the connections** to the supply and repeat, to get the negative half of the graph.

**The graph.** Plot current against potential difference. It is a **curve through the origin** that becomes **less steep** as the potential difference rises, and because reversing gives the mirror image, the whole graph is an **S shape**.

**Why.** A larger current makes the filament **hotter**. The resistance of a filament lamp **increases as its temperature increases**, so each extra volt produces **less** extra current than the one before — and the line flattens.

Say *in series* and *across*: naming the instruments without saying where they go scores only half.

examTechnique.body:
Write the equation before the numbers, then rearrange, then substitute. Showing the equation earns a method mark even if the arithmetic fails.

Check the time units in any Q = I t question. Minutes and hours are there to be converted.

Say where a meter is connected, not just its name: an ammeter in series, a voltmeter across the component.

When describing an I-V graph, name the shape and then say what it means about the resistance.

Use the words potential difference rather than voltage. Both are credited, but the mark schemes use the first.

For a required practical, name the instruments, say where each is connected, and say what is varied and what is measured.
examinerErrors: Leaving the time in minutes in Q = I t.
Connecting an ammeter across a component instead of in series.
Saying the gradient of an I-V graph is the resistance.
Saying a filament lamp's resistance falls as it heats up.
Confusing a thermistor with an LDR.
Describing an ohmic graph as a straight line without saying through the origin.
Drawing a resistor as a zigzag rather than a rectangle.
Saying current is used up by the components in a loop.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes the equation first and rearranges before substituting, so the method survives an arithmetic slip. It converts time units without being prompted. On graph questions it reads a point and divides rather than trusting the gradient, and when it does describe the gradient it knows it is one over the resistance. It explains the filament lamp curve by the causal chain — more current, hotter filament, higher resistance, less extra current — rather than stating that resistance changes. And it treats thermistor and LDR as one idea, more of the thing meaning less resistance, which halves what there is to remember.
